title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Vertical Scaling
summary: Vertical scaling (or "scaling up") means increasing the capacity of a single machine — adding more CPU cores, RAM, faster or larger disks, more network bandwidth — so that one node can handle more load, in contrast to…
objectives: Define vertical scaling and contrast it with horizontal scaling.
State Amdahl's Law and explain why it caps vertical scaling.
What are the downtime and availability implications of vertical scaling?
Why is vertical scaling called a "single point of failure," and how do you mitigate it?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Vertical scaling (or "scaling up") means increasing the capacity of a **single** machine — adding more CPU cores, RAM, faster or larger disks, more network bandwidth — so that one node can handle more load, in contrast to horizontal scaling (adding more machines) which spreads load across many nodes.

Vertical scaling is the simplest and often the first scaling strategy engineers reach for. When a service is slow, the immediate reflex is "give it a bigger box." This works because most software is written for a single machine and benefits immediately from more cores and memory without any code change. A Postgres instance that struggles on a 4-vCPU / 16-GB box will often run twice as fast on an 8-vCPU / 32-GB box, because the OS scheduler, the page cache, and the database's buffer pool all scale naturally with hardware. This is why cloud providers like AWS make it almost frictionless: AWS RDS supports in-place instance class upgrades from `db.m5.large` (2 vCPU, 8 GB) all the way to `db.m5.24xlarge` (96 vCPU, 384 GB) — a 48× jump in compute and memory on the same database engine.

Why does vertical scaling matter? Because it postpones the complexity of distributed systems. Horizontal scaling requires you to shard data, coordinate writes, handle cross-node consistency, deal with network partitions (CAP, Topic 10), and accept PACELC trade-offs (Topic 11). Vertical scaling avoids all of that — your single node remains a single source of truth, transactions stay ACID, and there is no partition to worry about. For many workloads, vertical scaling is the right answer for years: a reasonably-sized Postgres or Redis instance on a 32-core / 256-GB machine can serve tens of thousands of QPS and store terabytes of data, comfortably handling the needs of most SaaS products through Series B.

The canonical real-world example is **AWS RDS at Netflix and Amazon**. Amazon's own retail checkout and Netflix's billing services ran on vertically-scaled RDS Postgres instances for years before needing horizontal sharding. The pattern: start small (`db.r5.large`), monitor CPU and memory pressure, and bump up (`db.r5.4xlarge`, then `db.r5.24xlarge`) as load grows. Each upgrade is a brief maintenance-window reboot — typically under 10 minutes of downtime — and the database returns with 4× to 8× more capacity. Netflix famously runs Cassandra for high-throughput workloads (horizontal scaling), but their lower-throughput relational services — billing, configuration, user account — are still on vertically scaled RDS instances, because the operational simplicity is worth the cost.

Vertical scaling has hard limits, however. The largest AWS instance today is `u-7tb1.112xlarge` (448 vCPU, 7 TB RAM) — you cannot exceed that on a single node. Even at smaller scales, **Amdahl's Law** bites: if your workload is 95% parallelizable, going from 16 to 64 cores only yields a ~3.6× speedup, not 4×, because the 5% serial portion dominates. Database engines have non-parallelizable paths (lock acquisition, WAL flush, commit ordering) that cap the benefit of adding cores — a Postgres instance rarely uses more than ~40–60 cores effectively, even on a 96-core box. Memory has a similar diminishing return: the buffer pool hit rate asymptotes at some size, and adding RAM beyond that does nothing.

A critical pitfall is **downtime cost**. Vertical scaling on most cloud platforms requires a reboot — the instance stops on the old hardware and starts on the new. For AWS RDS this is typically 5–10 minutes; for EC2 it can be longer because the EBS volumes must detach and reattach. During this window the service is unavailable unless you have a multi-AZ standby. AWS RDS Multi-AZ makes this seamless — the standby is upgraded first and a failover promotes it — but the failover itself takes 60–120 seconds. For a Tier-1 service with a 99.99% availability SLO, even one such upgrade per quarter consumes a meaningful chunk of your error budget. Some workloads simply cannot tolerate scheduled reboots and must scale horizontally instead.

Another pitfall is the **single point of failure**. A vertically scaled service runs on one machine (or one primary plus a passive standby). If that machine fails — hardware fault, AZ outage, kernel panic — the entire service goes down until the standby is promoted or a new instance is provisioned. AWS's 2017 us-east-1 outage took down many services that depended on a single vertically-scaled RDS instance in that AZ. Horizontal scaling across AZs and regions is the only way to survive AZ-level failures with no downtime. The CAP and PACELC trade-offs (Topics 10 and 11) are the price of that horizontal distribution.

Cost is also non-linear. Cloud providers charge exponentially for the largest instance types — a `db.m5.24xlarge` costs roughly 48× a `db.m5.large`, but a 48× performance gain is rarely achieved because of Amdahl's Law and I/O bottlenecks. At some point, sharding across many smaller instances is cheaper per unit of capacity. The break-even point depends on the workload; for OLTP databases it is often around 16–32 cores, beyond which horizontal sharding wins on cost-per-QPS.

Vertical scaling connects to the rest of the curriculum as the *baseline* against which horizontal scaling is compared. It is the strategy that preserves **consistency** (single source of truth), avoids **latency** penalties (no cross-node coordination), and keeps **throughput** scaling linearly with hardware until Amdahl's Law kicks in. It is bounded by **availability** (single SPOF), **fault tolerance** (one failure = total outage), and **durability** (replication still needed for backup). The decision between vertical and horizontal is the first scaling decision every system designer makes, and the right answer is almost always "vertical until you can't, then horizontal."

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Service slow on small instance]
    Start --> Q{Can single node handle 2x peak load?}

    Q -->|Yes| VS[Vertical Scale: bump instance class]
    Q -->|No| HS[Horizontal Scale: shard / add replicas]

    VS --> VS1[db.m5.large -> db.m5.4xlarge -> db.m5.24xlarge]
    VS --> VS2[Amdahl limit ~ 40-60 cores effective for DB]
    VS --> VS3[Single SPOF: needs Multi-AZ standby]
    VS --> VS4[Reboot required: 5-10 min downtime or 60-120s failover]

    HS --> HS1[Shard by key / add read replicas]
    HS --> HS2[CAP + PACELC tradeoffs apply]
    HS --> HS3[Higher operational complexity]
    HS --> HS4[Survives AZ failure with no downtime]

    style VS fill:#cfc,stroke:#060
    style HS fill:#fcc,stroke:#600
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   VERTICAL SCALING (scale UP)             HORIZONTAL SCALING (scale OUT)
   -----------------------------           ------------------------------
                                                  +------+
       +---------------------+                    | N1   |
       | Big Box             |                    | ...  |
       |  96 vCPU            |       vs           | N2   |
       |  384 GB RAM         |                    +------+
       |  10 TB NVMe         |                    | N3   |
       |  (single SPOF)      |                    | ...  |
       +---------------------+                    | N4   |
                                                  +------+
   Pros: simple, ACID preserved               Pros: no SPOF, survives AZ failure
         no code change                              scales indefinitely
         no coordination latency                Cons: CAP/PACELC tradeoffs
   Cons: hardware ceiling                            sharding complexity
         single point of failure                     coordination overhead
         reboot downtime                             consistency model choice
         non-linear cost

   Amdahl's Law in vertical scaling:
   Speedup = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N)
   P = parallel fraction, N = cores
   +--------------------------------------------+
   | P=0.95, N=16:  speedup ~ 10.8x             |
   | P=0.95, N=64:  speedup ~ 15.4x (not 64x)   |
   | P=0.95, N=256: speedup ~ 17.8x (cap)       |
   +--------------------------------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. The service shows signs of strain — CPU sustained above 70%, memory pressure, slow queries. The first lever is to bump the instance class on the existing single node: `db.m5.large` → `db.m5.4xlarge`. This typically yields 4× compute and memory with one reboot.
2. If load keeps growing and you reach the largest practical instance (`db.m5.24xlarge` or `db.r5.24xlarge`), Amdahl's Law caps further gains from adding cores. Database engines particularly struggle past ~40–60 cores due to lock contention and serial commit paths.
3. At that point, vertical scaling is exhausted. You must scale horizontally: shard the data, add read replicas, or move to a distributed database. This introduces CAP and PACELC trade-offs, but it is the only way to grow beyond a single machine's ceiling while surviving AZ-level failures.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling decision helper.
- Amdahl's Law: speedup = 1 / ((1-p) + p/n).
- Find N where speedup stops scaling (gain < 5% per doubling).
- Rule 1: if strict ACID is required AND data fits on one box, prefer vertical
- Rule 2: if AZ failure tolerance required, MUST be multi-AZ (horizontal replication)
- Rule 3: availability SLO above 99.95% cannot tolerate scheduled reboot windows
- Rule 4: Amdahl ceiling check — estimate parallel fraction for typical OLTP
- Most OLTP DBs have ~0.85-0.90 parallel fraction due to lock contention

**Defines:** `Workload`, `Recommendation`, `amdahl_speedup()`, `estimate_max_vcpus_useful()`, `recommend()`

```python
"""
Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling decision helper.
Given workload characteristics, recommend a strategy.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List

@dataclass
class Workload:
    name: str
    peak_qps: int
    data_size_gb: int
    requires_strict_acid: bool          # multi-row transactions?
    availability_slo_percent: float     # e.g., 99.99
    az_failure_tolerance_required: bool # must survive AZ outage with no downtime?
    current_vcpus: int
    current_ram_gb: int

@dataclass
class Recommendation:
    strategy: str                # 'VERTICAL' | 'HORIZONTAL' | 'HYBRID'
    reasoning: List[str]
    suggested_next_step: str

def amdahl_speedup(p: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Amdahl's Law: speedup = 1 / ((1-p) + p/n)."""
    if n <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return 1.0 / ((1.0 - p) + p / n)

def estimate_max_vcpus_useful(workload_parallel_fraction: float) -> int:
    """Find N where speedup stops scaling (gain < 5% per doubling)."""
    n = 1
    while n < 1024:
        s_now = amdahl_speedup(workload_parallel_fraction, n)
        s_next = amdahl_speedup(workload_parallel_fraction, n * 2)
        gain = (s_next - s_now) / s_now if s_now > 0 else 0
        if gain < 0.05:
            return n
        n *= 2
    return n

def recommend(workload: Workload) -> Recommendation:
    reasons = []

    # Rule 1: if strict ACID is required AND data fits on one box, prefer vertical
    max_single_node_gb = 7_000  # largest AWS u-instance is ~7 TB RAM
    if workload.requires_strict_acid and workload.data_size_gb < max_single_node_gb:
        reasons.append("Strict ACID required and data fits on one node — vertical preserves transactions")
        strategy = "VERTICAL"
    elif workload.requires_strict_acid:
        reasons.append("Strict ACID + data exceeds single-node — need distributed ACID (Spanner/CockroachDB) or app-level saga")
        strategy = "HORIZONTAL"
    else:
        strategy = "HORIZONTAL"

    # Rule 2: if AZ failure tolerance required, MUST be multi-AZ (horizontal replication)
    if workload.az_failure_tolerance_required:
        reasons.append("AZ-failure tolerance required — needs multi-AZ replicas (horizontal)")
        strategy = "HORIZONTAL" if strategy == "VERTICAL" else strategy

    # Rule 3: availability SLO above 99.95% cannot tolerate scheduled reboot windows
    if workload.availability_slo_percent >= 99.99 and strategy == "VERTICAL":
        reasons.append("SLO ≥ 99.99% cannot tolerate vertical-scaling reboot windows — needs active-active horizontal")
        strategy = "HORIZONTAL"

    # Rule 4: Amdahl ceiling check — estimate parallel fraction for typical OLTP
    # Most OLTP DBs have ~0.85-0.90 parallel fraction due to lock contention
    amdahl_ceiling = estimate_max_vcpus_useful(workload_parallel_fraction=0.88)
    if workload.current_vcpus >= amdahl_ceiling and strategy == "VERTICAL":
        reasons.append(f"Amdahl ceiling reached (~{amdahl_ceiling} vCPUs effective) — vertical exhausted")
        strategy = "HORIZONTAL"

    # Suggested next step
    if strategy == "VERTICAL":
        suggested = f"Bump instance class: target ~2x current ({workload.current_vcpus * 2} vCPU, {workload.current_ram_gb * 2} GB)."
    elif strategy == "HORIZONTAL":
        suggested = "Shard by hot key (e.g., user_id) OR add read replicas for read-heavy workloads."
    else:
        suggested = "Hybrid: vertically scale critical path, horizontally shard cold paths."

    return Recommendation(strategy=strategy, reasoning=reasons, suggested_next_step=suggested)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    workloads = [
        Workload("Billing DB",        peak_qps=2_000,  data_size_gb=500,
                 requires_strict_acid=True,  availability_slo_percent=99.95,
                 az_failure_tolerance_required=False, current_vcpus=8,  current_ram_gb=32),
        Workload("Ad targeting",      peak_qps=200_000, data_size_gb=5_000,
                 requires_strict_acid=False, availability_slo_percent=99.99,
                 az_failure_tolerance_required=True,  current_vcpus=64, current_ram_gb=256),
        Workload("User sessions",     peak_qps=50_000, data_size_gb=200,
                 requires_strict_acid=False, availability_slo_percent=99.99,
                 az_failure_tolerance_required=True,  current_vcpus=16, current_ram_gb=64),
        Workload("Config service",    peak_qps=5_000,  data_size_gb=10,
                 requires_strict_acid=True,  availability_slo_percent=99.9,
                 az_failure_tolerance_required=False, current_vcpus=4,  current_ram_gb=16),
    ]

    for w in workloads:
        r = recommend(w)
        print(f"\n=== {w.name} ===")
        print(f"  Strategy: {r.strategy}")
        for reason in r.reasoning:
            print(f"    - {reason}")
        print(f"  Next step: {r.suggested_next_step}")

    print("\n--- Amdahl's Law reference (P=0.88, OLTP-like) ---")
    for n in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
        s = amdahl_speedup(0.88, n)
        print(f"  N={n:>4} cores → speedup={s:.2f}x")
```

quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up) means increasing the capacity of a single machine — more CPU, more RAM, faster disks, more network bandwidth. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more machines that share the load. Vertical scaling preserves single-node semantics: ACID transactions, single source of truth, no coordination overhead, no CAP/PACELC trade-offs.
